paper_title: OfficeTown: Generative Organizations for Evolving Agent Intelligence

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: AI agents increasingly use files and software tools to produce professional deliverables. Such work draws on materials, decisions, and feedback accumulated across assignments. We introduce OfficeTown, a generative simulation framework for professional organizations in which tasks and their context arise from continuing organizational work. From a natural-language description of an organization's purpose and activities, OfficeTown initializes an organization whose members coordinate work, delegate bounded assignments to assistant agents, and review their deliverables. Artifacts, decisions, and unresolved matters persist and shape subsequent work, while responsibilities and permissions determine what each member can see and do. We curate work requests, their context, and review feedback into executable resources for evaluation and learning. We construct OfficeTown Bench with 406 tasks and 4,836 evaluation criteria from 23 simulated organizations across eight professional domains, incorporating domain-expert feedback. Frontier-model evaluations reveal substantial remaining headroom. Supervised fine-tuning and on-policy distillation on OfficeTown data substantially improve Qwen3.5-9B on external professional-work benchmarks, including GDPval. Supplementary evaluations show that the principal--assistant harness achieves higher scores than the single- and multi-agent baselines tested. These results highlight the value of organizational simulation in generating work-grounded data and environments for the continued development of generalist agents.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Large language models are increasingly expected to produce professional deliverables using files, software tools, and organizational knowledge. Recent benchmarks (Patwardhan et al., 2025) and environment-synthesis methods (Dong et al., 2026) provide valuable resources for evaluating these capabilities, but typically treat tasks as isolated instances. Real professional work is rarely isolated. In organizations, assignments arise from ongoing activity rather than appearing independently. Deliverables are reviewed and revised, decisions create follow-up requests, and materials accumulated in one project become inputs to later work. Tasks therefore emerge from continuing process in which work products and work context co-evolve. This observation suggests different perspective. Instead of generating standalone tasks, we may seek to model the system that continuously produces professional work. Such system would naturally generate new assignments, contextual materials, review feedback, and long-range dependencies, offering scalable source of both evaluation and training data. Professional organizations are precisely such systems. We therefore introduce OfficeTown, generative simulation framework for professional organizations. From natural-language description of an organizations purpose and activities, OfficeTown constructs persistent organizational structures, roles, resources, and authority boundaries, then simulates ongoing work as professionals coordinate, 1 Figure 1: OfficeTown models ongoing work in persistent, permissioned organization. Professionals coordinate requests and review deliverables; assistants execute within authorized workspaces. Private drafts, revisions and unresolved matters carry context into subsequent work. The ten-role Juniper scene and its work links are illustrative. The lower plot shows cumulative materials from one Juniper organization over 181 simulated days (not wall-clock time): 27 initial files and 470 subsequent logical outputs, with revisions and exact copies deduplicated (Appendix A.7). These counts track material accumulation, not task quality or success. The right-hand panel shows synthetic inputs and the request for retained scope-and-routing memo, not model response. delegate, review, and follow up on assignments. Organizational state is persistent but not globally observable: each member has permission-filtered view determined by role, ownership, and sharing rules, and acts within their role-specific authority. Figure 1 illustrates Juniper instance. These professionals act as principals who coordinate work, delegate bounded assignments to assistant agents, and review their deliverables. Assistants execute within authorized workspaces. Artifacts and decisions update organizational state, while unresolved matters prompt follow-up work. We package selected assignments with their task-time context into executable resources for evaluation and learning. Figure 1 (right) shows concrete assignment with supporting materials and requested internal scope and routing memo. We construct OfficeTown Bench with 406 tasks and 4,836 evaluation criteria from 23 simulated organizations across eight professional domains, incorporating domain-expert feedback into task and rubric refinement. Delegating professionals span 139 distinct job titles. Training resources comprise 2,202 demonstrations for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and 828 taskenvironment pairs for on-policy distillation (OPD). Frontier-model evaluations reveal substantial remaining headroom on OfficeTown Bench. Training on OfficeTown data improves Qwen3.5-9B on external professional-work benchmarks. On 79 shared GDPval tasks, its rubric score rises from 65.75 to 73.65 after SFT and OPD. Supplementary evaluations favor the principalassistant harness over tested singleand multi-agent baselines. Our contributions are: We introduce generative simulation framework for professional organizations in which persistent, permissioned state shapes subsequent work. 2 We construct an expert-informed professional-work benchmark and training resources from ongoing organizational work. We demonstrate that the resulting tasks challenge frontier models and that OfficeTown data improves performance on external benchmarks.

sections.title: FRAMEWORK
sections.content: OfficeTown initializes an organization with roles, goals, resources, and authority, then simulates ongoing professional work progressing asynchronously (Figure 2). Requests, messages, commitments, and unresolved matters activate professionals, who coordinate work and delegate bounded assignments to assistants. They review delivered artifacts, request revisions, and arrange follow-up work. Files, communications, and decisions update persistent, permissioned organizational state throughout this process, shaping subsequent assignments.

sections.title: 2.1 ORGANIZATIONS, ROLES, AND AUTHORITY
sections.content: An OfficeTown instance represents professional organization or team initialized from naturallanguage description of its purpose and activities (Figure 2a). The description guides organizational objectives, professional roles, and reporting relationships. Each role defines continuing responsibilities and role-specific authority: which matters the professional handles and what they may execute, delegate, approve, or share. Figure 2d shows Juniper Financial Modelling, twelve-role instance. Each role is represented by model-driven professional whose profile draws on O*NET and ESCO occupational descriptions. Professionals act as principals responsible for ongoing work across assignments; assistants perform delegated executions. The organization starts with documents and data, termed the seed. These combine retrieved or adapted public sources with organization-specific synthetic records, preserving source references and the distinction between these origins. The seed provides initial working context that subsequent work can extend or revise. Appendices A.1A.2 detail construction, role skills, and Junipers setup. 2.2 PERSISTENT AND PERMISSIONED ORGANIZATIONAL STATE Organizational state includes personal working files, shared materials, communications, commitments, and pending decisions. Each professional maintains persistent workspace (Figure 2e) and structured work records separate from active conversation context, so refreshing model session does not erase unresolved work. Each activation presents selected work records alongside current requests, prioritizing outstanding commitments and discussions awaiting response. This state is persistent but not globally observable. Role permissions, ownership, sharing rules, and confidentiality determine each members information view; role-specific authority determines what they may do with it. Reporting relationships do not automatically grant file access. Assistants receive writable working files and permission-filtered, read-only shared references within the principals authorization, not access to other professionals private workspaces. Saving, accepting, and sharing deliverable are distinct actions. Saving retains files, including drafts and pending revisions; professional review determines acceptance; explicit sharing makes an accepted deliverable available to authorized recipients. Thus, saved work need not be accepted or visible to others. Acceptance, version, classification, and recipient permissions are checked before broader publication. Appendices A.4A.6 cover workspace checks, sessions, and recovery. 2.3 COORDINATION, DELEGATION, AND REVIEW Work follows shared simulated calendar, with professionals activated asynchronously by incoming requests, messages, meetings, follow-ups, or assistant deliveries (Figure 2b). The simulation controls activation and permitted actions; the professionals model decides how to respond using current requests, commitments, and accessible materials. Several matters can therefore progress concurrently. Appendix A.6 details scheduling and clock control. 3 Figure 2: OfficeTowns organizational simulation. (a) Organizational objectives, roles, and seed materials establish an organization. (b) Coordination, delegation, execution, and review connect ongoing work through retained materials and follow-up assignments. (c) Tasks drawn from this activity provide fixed inputs and executable environments for training and evaluation. (d) The recorded twelve-role hierarchy of Juniper Financial Modelling; the senior modellers computer is highlighted. (e) Filesystem and terminal views used by an assistant. The reconciliation and Juniper examples are separate. Directory names are verified; interfaces and terminal activity are schematic. When responsibilities intersect, members exchange permitted materials, question assumptions, and seek colleagues input. Team leads can meet to clarify objectives, identify missing inputs, and allocate responsibilities; meetings are not required for every assignment. Agreed work is recorded as requests specifying the intended outcome, responsible person, supporting materials, and deadline. Appendix A.3 provides recorded example. For delegated execution, the principal specifies the objective, available inputs, constraints, and expected deliverable. The assistant works within the authorized workspace and can ask the principal to clarify requirements or consult colleagues. On delivery, the principal inspects the actual artifact and decides whether to accept it, request revisions, or seek further information. Review can change both deliverable requirements and the work that other members need to undertake. These reviews are organizational decisions within the simulated organization, not independent benchmark judgments. Revisions build on submitted artifacts and review comments. Accepted results can become inputs to authorized colleagues work, while unresolved questions remain available for later investigation. These updates link assignments through accumulated context, extending work beyond the initial seed. Appendix A.7 illustrates material accumulation over six simulated months. 2.4 FROM ONGOING WORK TO EXECUTABLE TASKS An executable task pairs work request with materials available to its responsible professional when the work was assigned (Figure 2c). This task-time snapshot preserves both temporal and permission boundaries: personal files, authorized shared resources, and existing artifacts needed for revision may be included, but later solutions and evaluator-only information are excluded. Each attempt starts in fresh workspace initialized from these fixed inputs, where the agent can inspect and edit files, execute commands, and use the provided interfaces. The continuing organization is the source of the assignment; individual evaluation or learning attempts do not require replaying its entire history. Section 3 explains selection, expert-informed refinement, and packaging into benchmark and training resources.

EnterpriseBench, CRMArena-Pro, and AutomationBench examine crossfunctional workflows, access constraints, and policy-governed interaction (Vishwakarma et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025; Shepard & Salimans, 2026). ClawMark includes multi-day workflows with externally changing service state (Meng et al., 2026). Closest to our setting, TheAgentCompany combines simulated company, office applications, and model-driven colleagues with manually curated tasks (Xu et al., 2024). Environment and Task Synthesis Environment synthesis scales the construction of executable tasks and training resources. ScaleEnv generates tool environments and rollout-verified tasks, while EnvFactory builds stateful environments and training trajectories from API resources (Tu et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026b). EnvScaler, AWM, and AutoForge automate environment and verifiabletask construction (Song et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026; Cai et al., 2025). Agent-World combines synthesis with iterative reinforcement learning (Dong et al., 2026), and ClawEnvKit generates tasks, tools, and scoring criteria from natural-language requests (Li et al., 2026a). ScienceBuddy derives executable tasks and rubrics from researcher collaboration (Xue et al., 2026). Our focus is work generation, not recursive self-improvement (Duan et al., 2026). Generative Agents and Organizational Simulation Generative Agents uses memory, reflection, and planning to sustain social activity (Park et al., 2023). SOTOPIA studies goal-directed social interaction (Zhou et al., 2024b), while τ -bench evaluates policy-constrained tool use with simulated users (Yao et al., 2024). Agent Hospital connects institutional simulation with professional capability development through accumulated medical cases and reflection, without updating the underlying models (Li et al., 2024). OfficeTown connects organizational simulation with executable environment generation. Earlier artifacts, decisions, and unresolved matters shape subsequent work, while roles, ownership, and sharing rules scope the information and authority available for each assignment. This persistent, permissioned process generates tasks, context, and feedback for evaluation and training.

sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK
sections.content: OfficeTown models professional organizations as persistent, permissioned, and evolving work systems. Tasks, contextual materials, and feedback arise from ongoing work, rather than being constructed as isolated instances. Benchmark evaluations reveal gap between partial fulfillment and complete professional delivery, while training results demonstrate the learning value of the generated work on external benchmarks. Looking ahead, we will extend these simulations to more professional domains and institutional settings, with richer interactions, longer-running workflows, and collaboration across organizations. We will also investigate how persistent history, scoped access, and review shape task generation 9 and learning outcomes. Improving simulation fidelity and efficiency, and validating simulated work against real professional practice, will be important as these systems expand. Ethics Statement. OfficeTown uses referenced public sources, adapted materials, and synthetic records; it does not use private customer records. Domain experts contributed feedback on tasks and rubrics, and we report their contributions in aggregate. Occupational taxonomies and generative models can encode social and professional biases, so simulated organizations are examples rather than authoritative representations of occupations, institutions, or demographic groups. Toolusing agents can create privacy, security, and operational risks. In OfficeTown, agents operate within permission-scoped workspaces and synthetic authority; they are not used for real-world financial, legal, clinical, employment, or external-release decisions. Releases should preserve source attribution and licensing, remove sensitive operational information, and document intended use and limitations. OfficeTown is the name of this research project, not Microsoft Office product.

sections.title: A ORGANIZATION CONSTRUCTION AND SIMULATION
sections.content: A.1 CREATING AN ORGANIZATION FROM NATURAL-LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION construction request combines description of the organizations purpose and activities (as short as one sentence) with optional settings for organization size, language, and simulation period. OfficeTown expands the request into scope of work, departments, roles, reporting relationships, and synthetic customers. In the Juniper example (Figure 7a), departments divide client engagement, analytical work, data preparation, and review. Figure 7: generated office and one professional in detail. (a) Junipers 12 professionals, grouped by department, with examples of retrieved, adapted, and synthetic seed materials. The brief above is an excerpt of the full request, which also includes configuration. (b) Devon Aratas role, manager, profile, business authority, selected skills, and computer. The blue connector opens the highlighted persons details; it is not reporting relationship. Profiles and skills describe the generated configuration; files and saved work records show retained simulation state. The office layout, avatars, and terminal commands are illustrative. R/W denotes read/write access; R/O denotes read-only access, filtered by access-control rules (ACL). Professional roles are grounded in occupational descriptions from O*NET and ESCO. Each professional receives profile specifying their responsibilities, working style, schedule, and reporting relationships. Figure 7b expands one such role: Devon Arata, Senior Financial Modeller who reports to Analytical Production Director Nolan Voss. Devon is equipped with 15 professional and five general skill packages, including financial modelling and spreadsheet tools. Packages are selected from shared library, supplemented through skills.sh when needed, and retain their instructions and supporting resources. The expanded financial-modelling package contains instructions and two Python scripts. The role also defines what the professional is authorized to do. Devon can prepare internal models, run analysis scripts, and delegate work to an assistant, but cannot release material externally or operate real financial accounts. To build the seed, OfficeTown uses Web search to locate relevant professional guidance, reference documents, datasets, and worked examples. Retrieved materials are either retained in their original form or adapted to the organizations work. Synthetic records supply the organization-specific information needed to begin work, such as customer operating data, opening balances, and current business questions. The seed preserves the distinction between retrieved sources, adapted materials, and synthetic records, illustrated by the reference PDF, accounting workbook, and customer data in Figure 7a. Source references accompany the materials, while file-format and structural checks establish that the supplied assets can be read and used by the corresponding tools. These checks concern the materials accessibility and structure; professional judgments about their interpretation remain part of the simulated work. OfficeTown assembles the organization description, profiles, skill packages, and seed into runnable organization package. This package initializes personal workspaces, authorized shared resources, and the configured office services. A.2 EXAMPLE ORGANIZATION AND CONFIGURATION Juniper Financial Modelling (Figure 2) was constructed from brief whose business-specific portion begins: Juniper Financial Modelling provides management accounting, operating forecasts, cost analysis, cash-flow modelling and decision support to fictional small and mid-sized service, retail and project businesses. The remaining brief specifies the expected work products, review requirements, and use of synthetic customer records. Table 5 separates the generated organization properties from the settings used to construct and run the instance. Table 5: Generated properties and recorded settings of the Juniper instance. The simulation period is configured horizon, not measure of completed work. These settings are specific to this instance. Configuration Generated organization Initial synthetic customers Staffing target and limit Occupational references Recorded generation model Professional and assistant models Assistant execution Configured simulation period Clock policy Execution capacity Assistant timeout Clock checkpoint interval Service deployment Runtime security profile Run-level monitoring Additional semantic-memory backend Disabled Juniper instance 12 professionals; 7 departments; 11 reporting relationships 3 Target: 12; maximum: 16 O*NET 30.3; ESCO 1.2.1 GPT-5.5 GPT-5.5 Codex harness; worker containers; direct_home 1 January1 July 2026, 09:00 UTC; 181 days Adaptive business clock; maximum rate: 120 simulated seconds per wall-clock second Up to 6 concurrent professional turns; 4 assistant workers 1,200 seconds 5 seconds Isolated deployment (isolated_compose) legacy-dev Record-only The seed combines professional references and an adapted management-accounting workbook with three synthetic customer packets containing 34 groups of business records. References include the FAST Standard and the ICAEW Financial Modelling Code. Harborlights packet contains invoices, 16 payables, payroll records, dispatch jobs, opening balances, and recent bank activity, accompanied by control totals, source references, and unresolved assumptions. The Harborlight packet anchors the 13-week liquidity discussion in Figure 8, which is described next. A.3 COMMUNICATION AND WORK COORDINATION OfficeTown connects professionals to running office services through service-backed tools: Rocket.Chat for direct messages and team channels, Mailpit for email, and Baïkal for calendars and meeting scheduling. Deliveries are also recorded in persistent, recipient-specific inboxes, which the simulation uses to present incoming work. recipient receives the message and permitted references, not the senders private working context. The meeting organizer specifies the participants, time, and agenda. Each participant responds through their own model context, with preceding contributions supplied as part of the discussion. Turn-taking and explicit mentions determine who speaks next. Work agreed upon in conversation is recorded through explicit actions. Requests identify the intended outcome, responsible person, relevant materials, and deadline. professional can seek clarification, delegate execution to an assistant, or review returned deliverable. Meeting notes summarize the discussion, but do not themselves create an approval or mark an assignment as complete. These changes require the corresponding work actions. Figure 8 shows four consecutive turns from Juniper meeting about synthetic customers liquidity. Client engagement, data preparation, modelling, and review roles establish the required inputs, handoffs, forecast scenarios, and checks before execution. Figure 8: Professional coordination in simulated office. Four consecutive speaking turns from Juniper meeting about synthetic customers liquidity. Excerpts retain the original wording and order; ellipses mark omitted text. Side objects identify the proposed inputs, model, and review requirements, not completed or validated outputs. A.4 SESSIONS AND MEMORY Work records are stored independently of active conversation context. They retain commitments, ongoing discussions, unresolved decisions, and recent interactions with colleagues (Figure 9(b)). Commitments record what is owed and to whom; discussions identify who should respond next. Communication and work actions update these records through explicit requests and rule-based message cues. Clearing an incoming reminder does not mark the promised deliverable as complete. These structured records are distinct from the additional semantic-memory backend, which is disabled in the Juniper configuration  (Table 5)  . Only selected records enter each turn. Outstanding promises take priority over routine reminders, and discussions awaiting the professionals reply take priority over other exchanges. The default 17 limits are eight active commitments, five discussions, five unresolved decisions, and ten colleague records. Professionals can also maintain personal notes containing working assumptions, document references, and follow-up plans. Recent notes are included within separate size budget, while current project and request states are read from the simulations stored records. OfficeTown also supports an optional persistent-session mode for continuing coordination. The main session retains available conversation context alongside current requests and project state. Detailed inspections take place in branch of the same professionals session (Figure 9(a)). The branch inherits the current context and supports file inspection and tool use. In the illustrative forecast review, the professional identifies missing source links and requests revision. concise record of the conclusion, actions, and tools used returns to the main session, without retaining the full inspection in its active context. Figure 9: Continuing work through sessions and saved records. (a) In persistent-session mode, the same professional inspects returned forecast in review branch and brings its conclusion, actions, and brief tool record back into coordination. (b) Actions update work records; selected records and personal notes remain available when the context is refreshed under the same identifier on the next simulated day. (c) Compaction is optional; periodic triggering is off by default. The forecast, messages, and records form an illustrative example, not recorded Juniper interaction. At simulated day boundaries in this mode, the main context is refreshed by reopening the session under the same identifier with saved work records and current office state. The pending forecast revision in the illustration can therefore inform later turn without preserving the full earlier conversation. OfficeTown also supports optional compaction, which summarizes earlier exchanges while retaining recent messages (Figure 9(c)). Its periodic trigger is disabled by default. A.5 WORKSPACES, TOOLS, AND ACCESS CONTROL An assistant works in temporary execution container, while the principals computer workspace persists across assignments (Figure 10(a)). Professionals use this workspace to inspect and edit files, execute terminal commands, and access their skill packages. In direct-home mode, the runtime provides writable copy of the principals current home at /home/npc/computer, together with authorized shared references. runtime-generated instruction block identifies the principal and distinguishes writable files, read-only inputs, and temporary scratch space. Tasks requiring narrower access instead receive an isolated view with selected inputs and designated working and submission directories. Committed work remains in the professionals persistent workspace after the execution container is released. Shared materials are presented through separate, permission-filtered company view at /mnt/company. Ownership, role permissions, explicit sharing rules, and confidentiality classifications determine which documents appear in this view. reporting relationship does not grant unrestricted access to another persons files. Other professionals private homes are not mounted in the assistants environment. Shared documents are read-only: professionals and assistants can consult them or create their own working copies, but cannot directly overwrite the shared originals. File 18 Figure 10: bounded file view and persistent local changes. (a) In direct-home mode, an assistant receives writable copy of its principals home and permission-filtered, read-only company view. Other private homes are not mounted. R/W and R/O denote read/write and read-only access; ACL denotes access-control rules. (b) The runtime checks local changes before committing them; an interrupted commit can restore the preceding files and classification state. The files and changes are illustrative, not execution results. Recovery does not undo messages or other effects already sent to external services. operations and terminal execution enforce these boundaries through path checks, read-only mounts, and sandboxing. The revised workbook and new report in Figure 10(b) enter the persistent workspace only after the runtime checks protected paths, file validity, and the underlying workspace revision. Writers to the same professionals home are serialized to avoid conflicting updates. The runtime records the actual files created, modified, moved, or deleted, independently of the assistants completion report. The professional receives the deliverable locations, reported checks, and unresolved issues for review. Filesystem validation establishes what was saved; professional review determines whether the content meets the assignments requirements. For broader publication, the professional selects an accepted deliverable and its intended audience. The runtime checks the acceptance record, file version, classification, and recipient permissions before making it available to authorized colleagues. Personal working materials can therefore accumulate without exposing every intermediate draft to the whole organization. A.6 SIMULATION TIME AND RECOVERY Simulated time is managed separately from wall-clock execution time. When adaptive pacing is enabled, OfficeTown slows or pauses the simulated clock as unfinished work accumulates, then resumes its advance as the backlog decreases. The clock is periodically saved together with the runs original start and target times. resumed run continues toward that target rather than beginning another full simulation period. Routine activations follow working hours and meeting schedules; designated interruptions can receive earlier attention. Professionals act asynchronously within limits on concurrent model calls and assistant workers. Work awaiting capacity remains pending. Incoming messages remain in persistent inbox files, with acknowledgments tied to the exact source rows processed. Reading or queuing message does not acknowledge it as processed. partially processed batch retains acknowledgments even when rows finish out of order, leaving unprocessed rows available for later delivery. Capacity-deferred delegations retain their original identities and arguments when reconsidered for execution. Workspace recovery follows the checked-update boundary shown in Figure 10(b) and described in Section A.5. The runtime saves the preceding workspace state and journals an update before 19 committing changes. An interruption before commit leaves the persistent workspace unchanged; an interruption during commit can be recovered by restoring the saved files and classification metadata. The recovery is recorded explicitly. This mechanism applies to local workspace changes, not to reversing an email already sent or another external service action. The runtime also monitors its action bridge and model-session service and supports replacing failed services. When the simulation process remains alive, active sessions can be reopened using saved conversation records and retained session metadata. This reconstructs context for subsequent turns rather than resuming an interrupted model generation internally. Transient connection failures receive bounded retries, and unsuccessful attempts remain recorded. Run-level monitoring can stop execution on detected violations or record them while allowing an endurance run to continue. The latter policy leaves operation-level authorization and validation checks in force. At shutdown, the runtime stops new activity, allows bounded interval for ongoing work to settle, and reconciles assistant results with delivery records. Unfinished requests, failed attempts, and incomplete reviews remain in the saved state; reaching the target time does not mark them as finished. A.7 SIX-MONTH OFFICE SIMULATION We examine material accumulation in the Juniper instance over 181 simulated days, from 1 January to 1 July 2026. These dates and all checkpoints in Figure 11 follow the simulation clock (Section A.6), not elapsed wall-clock time. Materials are counted at their first recorded simulated delivery, with repeated revisions counted once. Figure 11(a) shows the cumulative collection growing from 27 initial files to 209, 376, and 497 files by simulated days 60, 120, and 181, respectively. The additional materials span documents and notes, data files, workbooks, and other formats. Figure 11(b) places these counts alongside selected materials available by each checkpoint: customer operating records, scenario workbook, retailproject source catalog, and reusable workbook component. This observation describes material accumulation; it does not assess deliverable quality or task success. 20 Figure 11: Work materials accumulated during six-month Juniper simulation. All dates and days denote simulated calendar time, not wall-clock runtime; the adaptive clock adjusts its rate to workprocessing pressure. (a) Cumulative material files: 27 distinct initial resource contents and 470 logical output files, counted at first simulated delivery. Revisions and recorded renames count once; exact copies are merged at first appearance. Navigation READMEs, explicit backups, and trash paths are excluded. Initial resources are grouped separately from subsequent outputs. (b) Selected material excerpts available by each date, redrawn from retained source versions; the final workbook contains synthetic scenario inputs. Counts describe the whole organization, not the illustrated folders.

sections.title: B DATA CONSTRUCTION AND BENCHMARK CASES
sections.content: B.1 RESOURCE MEMBERSHIP AND SEPARATION Figure 3, Table 1, and Tables 67 describe the same 406 benchmark tasks. Benchmark tasks, SFT demonstrations, and OPD environments have separate membership records; training-resource construction is described in Appendix E. Table 1 counts source organizations by their recorded organization identities, counting repeated simulations of the same identity once. Professional roles are distinct job titles of the primary delegating professionals, with case and whitespace normalized; they are not personnel counts or standardized occupational categories. Input-file counts include supplied company and personal-workspace files, historical service readbooks, and supplied service-state records. They exclude task-packaging metadata, runtime and evaluation files, and duplicate path aliases; an archive counts as one supplied file. Exposure to external task instances, answers, rubrics, and test feedback is distinct from using benchmarks format or methodology. B.2 EXPERT REVIEW To ground tasks and evaluation criteria in professional practice, we engaged 71 domain experts across eight professional domains during benchmark construction. Task-specific expertise requirements covered relevant specialization and occupational background, the ability to make independent professional judgments, and familiarity with native working materials and applicable standards. The construction-stage annotation records cover 1,051 candidate tasks and 32,274 rubric criteria. Among 1,011 recorded task-level familiarity assessments, 98.9% indicated that reviewers were familiar or very familiar with the assigned work. Experts assessed task realism and feasibility and examined rubric correctness, coverage, and importance, providing 3,842 criterion-level recommendations to edit, remove, merge, or split criteria. The annotations subsequently underwent separate review pass, combining expert assessment with follow-up quality control and producing refinement feedback traceable to individual tasks and criteria. The review instructions ask reviewers to assess task realism, objective clarity, input sufficiency, feasibility, deliverable clarity, permission boundaries, answer leakage, and unnecessary restrictions. Rubric review separately examines task alignment, professional correctness, assessability, clarity, redundancy, completeness, importance, evidence gaps, and valid alternative solutions. Reviewers record separate overall decisions for the task and rubric, with reasons and proposed revisions. For individual criteria, they can retain the standard or recommend the revisions described above, identify missing requirements, and assign the importance levels introduced in Section 3.2. These decisions concern the evaluation instrument, not an agents answer. Expertise or evidence limitations are recorded rather than treated as approval. Critical (P0) failures make the work essentially invalid or unusable; Major (P1) failures substantially affect its intended outcome or professional usability. Minor (P2) deficiencies do not substantially undermine the core outcome; Optional (P3) criteria describe desirable refinements with limited impact on overall success. Concrete edits remain linked to the reviewed task and criterion identities. For the final benchmark, historical expert feedback is bound to 394 of the 406 retained tasks; the other 12 have model-based review without bound human annotation.
